title: Carts That Stick Together
topic: Mathematical Routines · Momentum and energy in collisions

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: Cart A of mass 2m moves right with speed v0 toward cart B of mass m, which is at rest on a level track

Part A (i), Figure 2: Blank axes of momentum p_x versus time t with dashed vertical lines at t1 and t2

prompt: Cart A of mass \(2m\) moves to the right along a level, frictionless track with speed \(v_0\). Cart B of mass \(m\) is at rest. At time \(t_1\) the carts collide and stick together, and at \(t_2\) the combined carts move to the right with constant speed \(v_f\).

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 120" width="400" height="120" role="img" aria-label="Cart A of mass 2m moves right with speed v0 toward cart B of mass m, which is at rest on a level track" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="10" y1="95" x2="390" y2="95" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="60" y="55" width="90" height="34" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="105" y="77" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">2m</text><circle cx="80" cy="92" r="6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="130" cy="92" r="6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><line x1="155" y1="62" x2="196" y2="62" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.4"/><polygon points="205,62 196,66 196,58" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1"/><text x="180" y="54" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">v₀</text><rect x="260" y="61" width="64" height="28" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="292" y="80" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">m</text><circle cx="276" cy="92" r="6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="308" cy="92" r="6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="105" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Cart A</text><text x="292" y="115" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Cart B (at rest)</text></svg>
figures.alt: Cart A of mass 2m moves right with speed v0 toward cart B of mass m, which is at rest on a level track
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A (i)
parts.text: On axes like those in Figure 2, sketch the \(x\)-component of the total momentum \(p_x\) of the two-cart system as a function of time from \(t = 0\) until after \(t_2\).

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches \(p_x\) as constant before the collision \((t < t_1)\) or after it \((t > t_1)\).
commonErrors: draws momentum increasing or decreasing linearly
draws a spike or dip at the collision
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Draws a horizontal line before t1.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Draws a line that drops at t1 because cart A slows down.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches a single continuous, nonzero horizontal line from \(t = 0\) through and beyond \(t_2\), showing that the system's momentum never changes.
commonErrors: draws two different horizontal levels
draws a gap at the collision
draws the line at zero
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: One unbroken horizontal line at a positive value across the whole graph.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A step down at t1 to a lower horizontal line.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 340 200" width="340" height="200" role="img" aria-label="Blank axes of momentum p_x versus time t with dashed vertical lines at t1 and t2" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="40" y1="170" x2="311" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><polygon points="320,170 311,174 311,166" fill="currentColor" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="40" y1="180" x2="40" y2="29" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6"/><polygon points="40,20 44,29 36,29" fill="currentColor" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="30" y="26" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">pₓ</text><text x="325" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">t</text><text x="32" y="184" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">O</text><line x1="150" y1="30" x2="150" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="150" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">t₁</text><line x1="250" y1="30" x2="250" y2="170" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="250" y="186" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">t₂</text></svg>
figures.alt: Blank axes of momentum p_x versus time t with dashed vertical lines at t1 and t2
figures.caption: Figure 2

parts.label: A (ii)
parts.text: Derive an expression for \(v_f\) in terms of \(v_0\). Begin your derivation by writing a fundamental physics principle or an equation from the reference information.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes conservation of momentum, \(p_i = p_f\) (or \(\Sigma p_i = \Sigma p_f\)), as the starting principle.
commonErrors: starts with conservation of kinetic energy
starts with v = d/t
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Writes \(p_i = p_f\) and then \(2m v_0 = (2m + m)v_f\).
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Begins with ½(2m)v0² = ½(3m)vf², treating the collision as elastic.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sets \(2m v_0\) equal to the combined momentum \(3m\,v_f\) and solves \(v_f = \tfrac{2}{3}v_0\). A correct isolated final answer earns this point and the previous one.
commonErrors: uses 2m for the final mass
loses the factor of 2 on the initial momentum, getting v0/3

parts.label: A (iii)
parts.text: Derive an expression for the change in kinetic energy \(\Delta K\) of the two-cart system from \(t = 0\) to \(t_2\) in terms of \(m\), \(v_0\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Shows a multistep derivation that uses \(K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2\) beyond restating it, such as writing \(\Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}m_fv_f^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}m_iv_i^2\) with quantities substituted.
commonErrors: writes only K = ½mv² with nothing substituted
uses momentum in place of kinetic energy

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses \(2m\) as the moving mass before the collision and \(3m\) after it.
commonErrors: uses m or 2m for the final mass
includes cart B in the initial kinetic energy with a nonzero speed
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Uses ½(3m)v0² for the initial kinetic energy.

rubricPoints.criterion: Substitutes a \(v_f\) consistent with part A (ii) and reaches \(\Delta K = -\tfrac{1}{3}mv_0^2\) (or an answer consistent with an incorrect \(v_f\)).
commonErrors: reports a positive change in kinetic energy
arithmetic error with the fraction 4/9
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Reports ΔK = 0 because the collision conserves energy.

parts.label: B
parts.text: The experiment is repeated, but now cart B carries a light spring bumper, so the carts push on each other through the spring for a short time interval \(\Delta t\) before separating. Indicate whether the \(x\)-component of the total momentum of the two-cart system increases, decreases, or remains constant during \(\Delta t\). Justify your answer.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that the total momentum remains constant.
commonErrors: says the momentum decreases because cart A slows
says momentum is stored in the spring
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Decreases, because the spring absorbs momentum.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the spring force is internal to the two-cart system, or that the net external force on the system is zero.
commonErrors: mentions only that the track is frictionless without addressing the spring force
claims the spring force is external
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The spring forces are internal, and no net external force acts horizontally.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The spring pushes cart A backward, so momentum is lost.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the impulses (or changes in momentum) of the two carts are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, or relates the system’s change in momentum to the net external force.
commonErrors: states Newton’s third law without connecting it to momentum or impulse
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The spring exerts equal and opposite forces on the carts for the same time, so their impulses cancel.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The forces are equal and opposite.

sampleResponse: A (i) A horizontal line at \(p_x = 2mv_0\) from \(t = 0\) through and past \(t_2\). (ii) \(p_i = p_f\): \(2mv_0 = 3mv_f\), so \(v_f = \tfrac{2}{3}v_0\). (iii) \(\Delta K = \tfrac{1}{2}(3m)\left(\tfrac{2}{3}v_0\right)^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}(2m)v_0^2 = \tfrac{2}{3}mv_0^2 - mv_0^2 = -\tfrac{1}{3}mv_0^2\). B Remains constant. The spring forces on the two carts are internal to the system and equal and opposite, so their impulses are equal and opposite and the net external horizontal force is zero; the system's momentum cannot change.

title: Spring Launcher and Curved Ramp
topic: Translation Between Representations · Energy bar charts and conservation of energy

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: A spring attached to a wall on the left is compressed by a block at position 1. Position 2 is where the block leaves the relaxed spring. The level surface curves up into a ramp on the right; position 3 is at height H on the ramp

Part A, Figure 2: Position 2: energy bar chart with columns K, Ug, Us, showing K = 8E0, Ug = 0E0, Us = 0E0

Part A, Figure 3: Positions 1 and 3 (blank): energy bar chart with columns K, Ug, Us, all blank for the student to complete

prompt: A block of mass \(M\) is pushed against a horizontal spring of spring constant \(k\), compressing it a distance \(d\) from its relaxed length, and is released from rest at position 1. The block leaves the spring at position 2, slides along the level surface, and then up a curved ramp, momentarily stopping at height \(H\) at position 3. All surfaces are frictionless. The gravitational potential energy \(U_g\) of the block-spring-Earth system is zero when the block is on the level surface.

parts.label: A
parts.text: The bar chart in Figure 2 represents the energy of the block-spring-Earth system at position 2. On charts like those in Figure 3, draw bars to represent \(K\), \(U_g\), and \(U_s\) at position 1 and at position 3. Represent any energy that is zero with a distinct line on the zero line, and keep the heights consistent with the scale of Figure 2.

rubricPoints.criterion: At position 1, draws only a \(U_s\) bar (with \(K\) and \(U_g\) shown as zero).
commonErrors: draws a kinetic energy bar at position 1
includes U_g at position 1
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Position 1: U_s bar only; K and U_g drawn as lines on zero.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Position 1: equal K and U_s bars.

rubricPoints.criterion: At position 3, draws only a \(U_g\) bar (with \(K\) and \(U_s\) shown as zero).
commonErrors: draws a nonzero K at position 3
draws a U_s bar at position 3
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Position 3: U_g and K bars, as if the block is still moving.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws the single bar at each position with a height of \(8E_0\), equal to the total energy shown in Figure 2.
commonErrors: changes the total energy between positions
draws heights that do not match the 8E0 total
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Both the U_s bar at position 1 and the U_g bar at position 3 reach 8E0.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Starting with conservation of energy, derive an expression for \(H\) in terms of \(M\), \(k\), \(d\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes a multistep derivation beginning with conservation of energy for the block-spring-Earth system.
commonErrors: starts with kinematics equations
starts with Newton’s second law without energy

rubricPoints.criterion: Equates the spring potential energy at position 1 to the gravitational potential energy at position 3.
commonErrors: equates spring energy to kinetic energy and stops
adds the two energies instead of equating them

rubricPoints.criterion: Substitutes \(\tfrac{1}{2}kd^2\) for the spring energy or \(MgH\) for the gravitational energy.
commonErrors: uses kd without the square
uses ½kd for the spring energy

rubricPoints.criterion: Arrives at \(H = \dfrac{kd^2}{2Mg}\) or an algebraic equivalent.
commonErrors: drops the factor of 2
leaves H in terms of the speed at position 2

parts.label: C
parts.text: On axes of energy versus the block's position \(x\), from \(x = -d\) (position 1) to \(x = 0\) (position 2), sketch and label (i) the spring potential energy \(U_s\) and (ii) the kinetic energy \(K\) of the block.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches \(U_s\) as a concave-up curve that is maximum at \(x = -d\) and zero at \(x = 0\).
commonErrors: draws U_s as a straight line
draws U_s increasing toward x = 0
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: U_s is a decreasing parabola reaching zero at x = 0.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: U_s is a straight line from 8E0 to 0.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches \(K\) starting at zero at \(x = -d\) and increasing to its maximum at \(x = 0\), concave down.
commonErrors: draws K as constant
draws K decreasing
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: K starts at zero and rises to 8E0 at x = 0, curving downward.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws \(K\) and \(U_s\) so that their sum is constant at every position (the curves are mirror images).
commonErrors: curves cross at a value other than half the total
K reaches a maximum other than the total energy
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The curves cross at 4E0, halfway between.

parts.label: D
parts.text: The spring is now compressed a distance \(2d\). Indicate whether the new maximum height is greater than \(2H\), equal to \(2H\), or less than \(2H\). Justify your answer by referencing your derivation in part B.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that the new height is greater than \(2H\) (it is \(4H\)).
commonErrors: claims the height doubles
claims the height is unchanged

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies using the functional dependence \(H \propto d^2\) from part B, so doubling \(d\) quadruples \(H\).
commonErrors: states that more compression gives more height without the squared dependence
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Because H is proportional to d², doubling d multiplies H by 4.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: More compression stores more energy, so the block goes higher.

sampleResponse: A Position 1: \(U_s = 8E_0\), \(K = U_g = 0\). Position 3: \(U_g = 8E_0\), \(K = U_s = 0\). B \(E_1 = E_3\): \(\tfrac{1}{2}kd^2 = MgH\), so \(H = \dfrac{kd^2}{2Mg}\). C \(U_s\) decreases along a concave-up parabola from \(8E_0\) at \(x = -d\) to 0 at \(x = 0\); \(K\) rises from 0 to \(8E_0\), and the two always add to \(8E_0\). D Greater than \(2H\): since \(H \propto d^2\), compressing the spring twice as far stores four times the energy, so the block rises to \(4H\).

title: Finding a Spring Constant from Oscillations
topic: Experimental Design and Analysis · Simple harmonic motion and linearization

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Physics 1 Question 3 (Experimental Design and Analysis)

stimulus.content:
Figure 1: A cart on a level track is attached to a horizontal spring fixed to a wall on the left. Masses can be stacked on the cart

Part C, Table 1
Total mass m (kg) | Period T (s)
0.20 | 0.63
0.40 | 0.88
0.60 | 1.10
0.80 | 1.25
1.00 | 1.41

prompt: Students have a cart attached to a horizontal spring of unknown spring constant \(k\) on a level track with negligible friction, as shown in Figure 1. They have a set of masses that can be placed on the cart, a stopwatch, and a balance.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 110" width="380" height="110" role="img" aria-label="A cart on a level track is attached to a horizontal spring fixed to a wall on the left. figures.alt: A cart on a level track is attached to a horizontal spring fixed to a wall on the left. Masses can be stacked on the cart
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe an experimental procedure the students could use to collect data that would allow them to determine k using a linear graph. Include any steps needed to reduce experimental uncertainty.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes varying the total oscillating mass (cart plus added masses, measured with the balance) and measuring the period of oscillation for each mass.
commonErrors: varies the amplitude instead of the mass
measures only one mass
measures a distance with a stopwatch
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Add masses to the cart, measure the total mass, displace the cart, and time its oscillations for each mass.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Pull the cart back different distances and time how long it takes to return.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a reasonable way to reduce uncertainty, such as timing several oscillations and dividing, or repeating trials for each mass and averaging.
commonErrors: says "be careful" without a specific method
repeats only the mass measurement
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Time 10 oscillations and divide by 10, and repeat three times for each mass.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe how the data could be graphed to produce a linear graph and how the graph would be analyzed to determine k.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies quantities that produce a linear graph, such as \(T^2\) versus \(m\) (or \(T\) versus \(\sqrt{m}\)).
commonErrors: graphs T versus m and calls it linear
graphs T versus k
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Graph \(T^2\) on the vertical axis and the total mass \(m\) on the horizontal axis.

rubricPoints.criterion: Relates the slope to \(k\), for example: slope \(= \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}\), so \(k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{slope}}\).
commonErrors: says the slope equals k
inverts the relationship
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The slope is the spring constant.

parts.label: C
parts.text: The students' data are shown in Table 1. (i) Indicate a quantity that could be graphed on the vertical axis, with total mass on the horizontal axis, to produce a linear graph. (ii) Plot the data on a labeled graph with a linear scale and units. (iii) Draw a best-fit line.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates \(T^2\) (or an equivalent such as \(T^2/4\pi^2\)) for the vertical axis.
commonErrors: chooses T
chooses 1/T

rubricPoints.criterion: Labels the vertical axis with the quantity and correct units and uses a linear scale.
commonErrors: omits units
uses an uneven scale
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Labels the axis "T² (s²)" with evenly spaced ticks.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: No label on the vertical axis.

rubricPoints.criterion: Plots points consistent with the indicated quantities (about 0.40, 0.77, 1.21, 1.56, 1.99 s² for \(T^2\)).
commonErrors: plots T instead of the squared values
misplots two or more points

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws a single straight best-fit line that follows the trend of the data rather than connecting the dots.
commonErrors: connects the points dot to dot
forces the line through the first and last points only
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A straight line with points scattered on both sides.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Total mass m (kg) 0.20, Period T (s) 0.63; Total mass m (kg) 0.40, Period T (s) 0.88; Total mass m (kg) 0.60, Period T (s) 1.10; Total mass m (kg) 0.80, Period T (s) 1.25; Total mass m (kg) 1.00, Period T (s) 1.41

parts.label: D
parts.text: Using your best-fit line, calculate an experimental value for k.

rubricPoints.criterion: Correctly relates the slope of the best-fit line to \(k\), consistent with the graph in part C.
commonErrors: uses a single data point instead of the slope
uses the slope directly as k
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: k = T²/m from the first row.

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports a value of \(k\) between about \(18\) and \(22\text{ N/m}\).
commonErrors: reports k in the wrong units
reports about 2 N/m by inverting the slope

sampleResponse: A For several total masses (measured with the balance), pull the cart a small distance, release it, and time 10 complete oscillations; divide by 10 to find \(T\). Repeat three times per mass and average. B Graph \(T^2\) versus \(m\); because \(T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}m\), the slope is \(\dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}\), so \(k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{slope}}\). C Vertical axis \(T^2\) (s²); points (0.20, 0.40), (0.40, 0.77), (0.60, 1.21), (0.80, 1.56), (1.00, 1.99) with a straight best-fit line. D Slope \(\approx 1.99\text{ s}^2\text{/kg}\), so \(k \approx 4\pi^2/1.99 \approx 20\text{ N/m}\).

title: Weighing a Block Under Water and Oil
topic: Qualitative/Quantitative Translation · Buoyant force and Newton’s second law

stimulus.content: Figure 1: Two containers. In each, a block hangs fully submerged from a spring scale above. The left container holds water; the right container holds oil

prompt: A block of mass \(m\) and volume \(V\) hangs at rest from a spring scale. In Scenario 1, the block is fully submerged in water of density \(\rho_w\), and the scale reads \(F_1\). In Scenario 2, the same block is fully submerged in oil of density \(\rho_o\), where \(\rho_o < \rho_w\), and the scale reads \(F_2\). The block does not touch the bottom of either container.

In each, a block hangs fully submerged from a spring scale above. The left container holds water; the right container holds oil" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="35" y="70" width="110" height="105" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="36" y="85" width="108" height="89" stroke="#60a5fa" stroke-width="0.1" fill="#60a5fa"/><rect x="82" y="8" width="16" height="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><line x1="90" y1="48" x2="90" y2="112" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><rect x="74" y="112" width="32" height="28" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="90" y="188" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Water, ρw</text><rect x="235" y="70" width="110" height="105" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="236" y="85" width="108" height="89" stroke="#60a5fa" stroke-width="0.1" fill="#60a5fa"/><rect x="282" y="8" width="16" height="40" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><line x1="290" y1="48" x2="290" y2="112" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><rect x="274" y="112" width="32" height="28" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="290" y="188" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Oil, ρo</text></svg>
figures.alt: Two containers. In each, a block hangs fully submerged from a spring scale above. The left container holds water; the right container holds oil
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Indicate whether \(F_1\) is greater than, less than, or equal to \(F_2\). Justify your answer in terms of all the forces exerted on the block, using qualitative reasoning beyond referencing equations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates \(F_1 < F_2\).
commonErrors: indicates F1 > F2
indicates the readings are equal

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the gravitational force on the block (its weight) is the same in both scenarios.
commonErrors: ignores the weight
says the block weighs less in water
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The block’s weight mg is the same in both liquids.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The block is lighter in water.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that the buoyant force is greater in the denser water, so the spring scale must supply less upward force to keep the block in equilibrium.
commonErrors: states the buoyant force depends on the block’s density
does not connect the buoyant force to the scale reading
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Water exerts a larger buoyant force because it is denser, so the scale supports less of the weight.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Starting with Newton's second law, derive an expression for the spring scale reading \(F\) when the block is fully submerged in a fluid of density \(\rho\). Express your answer in terms of \(m\), \(V\), \(\rho\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes Newton's second law for the block in equilibrium, \(\Sigma F = 0\), including the scale force, the buoyant force, and the weight.
commonErrors: omits the buoyant force
sets the net force equal to ma with a nonzero a

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses \(F_B = \rho V g\) for the buoyant force.
commonErrors: uses the block’s density in the buoyant force
omits g

rubricPoints.criterion: Arrives at \(F = mg - \rho V g\) (or an algebraic equivalent).
commonErrors: sign error, getting mg + ρVg

parts.label: C
parts.text: Indicate whether your expression from part B is or is not consistent with your claim in part A. Briefly justify your answer by referencing the expression.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses functional dependence language to relate \(F\) and \(\rho\) in the derived expression.
commonErrors: restates part A without referencing the expression
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The reading decreases as \(\rho\) increases because \(\rho\) appears in a subtracted term.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: My answer agrees with part A.

rubricPoints.criterion: Correctly concludes that a larger fluid density gives a smaller reading, consistent with part A (or correctly identifies an inconsistency with an incorrect part A).
commonErrors: claims consistency when the expression contradicts part A
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Since \(\rho_w > \rho_o\), \(F_1 = mg - \rho_w V g < F_2\), which is consistent.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: It is consistent because both depend on mass.

sampleResponse: A \(F_1 < F_2\). Gravity pulls down on the block with the same force \(mg\) in both liquids, and each liquid pushes up with a buoyant force. Water is denser, so it pushes up harder; the scale then has to supply less upward force to hold the block at rest. B \(\Sigma F = 0\): \(F + \rho V g - mg = 0\), so \(F = mg - \rho V g\). C Consistent: \(\rho\) appears in a subtracted term, so a denser fluid gives a smaller reading, matching \(F_1 < F_2\).

title: Garden Hose Stream
topic: Mathematical Routines · Projectile motion and the continuity equation

stimulus.content: Figure 1: A nozzle at height h above the ground sprays water horizontally. The stream curves downward and lands a horizontal distance D away

prompt: Water leaves the nozzle of a garden hose horizontally at height \(h\) above level ground and lands a horizontal distance \(D\) from the nozzle, as shown in Figure 1. Air resistance is negligible. At \(t = 0\) a small parcel of water leaves the nozzle, and at \(t = t_f\) it reaches the ground.

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 400 170" width="400" height="170" role="img" aria-label="A nozzle at height h above the ground sprays water horizontally. The stream curves downward and lands a horizontal distance D away" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="10" y1="150" x2="390" y2="150" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="30" y="40" width="40" height="14" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><path d="M70 47 Q200 50 330 150" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="3"/><line x1="50" y1="54" x2="50" y2="150" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="40" y="105" text-anchor="end" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">h</text><line x1="70" y1="162" x2="330" y2="162" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8"/><text x="200" y="158" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">D</text><text x="50" y="32" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">nozzle</text></svg>
figures.alt: A nozzle at height h above the ground sprays water horizontally. The stream curves downward and lands a horizontal distance D away
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A (i)
parts.text: On separate axes, sketch graphs of the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity of the water parcel as functions of \(t\) from \(t = 0\) to \(t = t_f\). Take upward as positive.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches the horizontal velocity component as a nonzero horizontal line (constant) from 0 to t_f.
commonErrors: draws the horizontal velocity decreasing
starts it at zero
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A line sloping down to zero at t_f.

rubricPoints.criterion: Sketches the vertical velocity component as a straight line starting at zero and becoming increasingly negative (slope −g).
commonErrors: starts at a nonzero value
draws it curving
draws it positive
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A straight line from 0 sloping downward.

parts.label: A (ii)
parts.text: Derive an expression for the speed \(v_0\) of the water as it leaves the nozzle. Express your answer in terms of \(h\), \(D\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses vertical kinematics with zero initial vertical velocity, such as \(h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt_f^2\), to find the time of flight.
commonErrors: uses the horizontal speed in the vertical equation
assumes an upward launch

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses constant horizontal velocity, \(D = v_0 t_f\).
commonErrors: includes an acceleration in the horizontal direction

rubricPoints.criterion: Combines the equations to get \(v_0 = D\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}\) or an equivalent.
commonErrors: inverts the fraction under the root
drops the factor of 2

parts.label: A (iii)
parts.text: The nozzle has a circular opening of radius \(r\). Derive an expression for the volume flow rate of water leaving the nozzle in terms of \(h\), \(D\), \(r\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses volume flow rate \(= Av\) with \(A = \pi r^2\).
commonErrors: uses the circumference 2πr
uses r² without π

rubricPoints.criterion: Substitutes the speed from part A (ii) to obtain \(\pi r^2 D\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}\) (or an expression consistent with an earlier answer).
commonErrors: leaves v0 in the final answer
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: \(\pi r^2 v_0\) with v0 not expressed in terms of the given quantities.

parts.label: B
parts.text: A thumb is placed over part of the nozzle, reducing the area of the opening, while the volume flow rate stays the same. The water still leaves horizontally from height \(h\). Indicate whether the new landing distance is greater than, less than, or equal to \(D\). Justify your answer, including qualitative reasoning beyond mathematical expressions.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that the new landing distance is greater than D.
commonErrors: indicates less than D
indicates equal because the flow rate is unchanged

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that with the same volume of water per second passing through a smaller opening, the water must leave faster (continuity).
commonErrors: says the water has more pressure without relating it to speed
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The same volume per second must squeeze through a smaller area, so it leaves at a greater speed.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that the time in the air is unchanged because it depends only on the height, so a greater horizontal speed covers a greater distance.
commonErrors: claims the faster water also falls more slowly or quickly
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: It still falls the same height in the same time, but travels faster horizontally during that time.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: It goes farther because it is faster.

sampleResponse: A (i) Horizontal component: constant line at \(v_0\). Vertical component: straight line from 0 decreasing with slope \(-g\). (ii) \(h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt_f^2\), so \(t_f = \sqrt{2h/g}\); \(D = v_0t_f\), so \(v_0 = D\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}\). (iii) Flow rate \(= Av_0 = \pi r^2 D\sqrt{\dfrac{g}{2h}}\). B Greater than \(D\). The same volume of water per second must pass through a smaller opening, so it moves faster. The fall time depends only on \(h\), which is unchanged, so the faster water travels farther horizontally before landing.

title: Air-Track Glider Collision
topic: Translation Between Representations · Momentum vectors and center of mass motion

stimulus.content: Figure 1: Glider X of mass 2m0 moves right with speed v0 toward glider Y of mass m0 at rest on an air track

prompt: Glider X of mass \(2m_0\) moves to the right on a level air track with speed \(v_0\) toward glider Y of mass \(m_0\), which is at rest. Friction is negligible. At \(t = t_1\) they collide, and immediately afterward glider X moves to the right with speed \(\tfrac{1}{3}v_0\).

figures.svg: <svg class="ap-fig" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 380 110" width="380" height="110" role="img" aria-label="Glider X of mass 2m0 moves right with speed v0 toward glider Y of mass m0 at rest on an air track" font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><line x1="10" y1="80" x2="370" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="3"/><rect x="60" y="50" width="90" height="28" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="105" y="69" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">2m₀</text><line x1="155" y1="58" x2="191" y2="58" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="2.4"/><polygon points="200,58 191,62 191,54" fill="#3b82f6" stroke="#3b82f6" stroke-width="1"/><text x="178" y="50" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">v₀</text><rect x="250" y="54" width="60" height="24" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity=".14"/><text x="280" y="71" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-style="italic">m₀</text><text x="105" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Glider X</text><text x="280" y="100" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor" font-size="11">Glider Y (at rest)</text></svg>

figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Before the collision, glider X's momentum is represented by an arrow 6 grid units long pointing right, and glider Y's momentum is zero. Draw arrows, on the same scale, to represent the momentum of each glider immediately after the collision. Label any zero momentum "\(p = 0\)".

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws glider X’s momentum after the collision as a rightward arrow 2 units long.
commonErrors: draws X’s arrow pointing left
draws it 6 units long

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws glider Y’s momentum after the collision as a rightward arrow 4 units long.
commonErrors: draws Y’s arrow 6 units long
draws Y’s arrow pointing left

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws arrows whose lengths sum to 6 units, the same total momentum as before the collision.
commonErrors: changes the total momentum
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: X = 2 units and Y = 4 units, total 6.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Starting with conservation of linear momentum, derive an expression for the kinetic energy of glider Y immediately after the collision in terms of \(m_0\), \(v_0\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Writes conservation of momentum with the correct masses: \(2m_0v_0 = 2m_0\left(\tfrac{1}{3}v_0\right) + m_0v_Y\).
commonErrors: omits glider X’s final momentum
uses m0 for glider X

rubricPoints.criterion: Solves for \(v_Y = \tfrac{4}{3}v_0\).
commonErrors: gets 2v0 by ignoring X’s final momentum

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses \(K = \tfrac{1}{2}m_0v_Y^2\) to obtain \(K_Y = \tfrac{8}{9}m_0v_0^2\) (or a value consistent with the earlier speed).
commonErrors: uses glider X’s mass
forgets to square the speed

parts.label: C
parts.text: A graph shows the positions of glider X, glider Y, and the center of mass of the two-glider system from \(t = 0\) to \(t_1\): X's line rises with slope \(v_0\), Y's line is horizontal, and the center of mass line rises with a constant slope. Describe or sketch the three lines from \(t_1\) to \(2t_1\), clearly labeling each.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws glider Y's line after \(t_1\) as a straight line with the greatest positive slope (speed \(\tfrac{4}{3}v_0\)).
commonErrors: keeps Y horizontal after the collision

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws glider X's line after \(t_1\) as a straight line with a smaller positive slope (speed \(\tfrac{1}{3}v_0\)), continuous at \(t_1\).
commonErrors: draws X moving backward
draws a gap at t1
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: X continues rising, but less steeply.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws the center of mass line continuing with the same slope \(\left(\tfrac{2}{3}v_0\right)\) before and after \(t_1\).
commonErrors: changes the center of mass slope at t1
draws the center of mass at rest
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The center of mass line is one unbroken straight line.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The center of mass line bends at t1.

rubricPoints.criterion: Labels all three lines so they can be distinguished, with the center-of-mass line lying between the lines for X and Y after \(t_1\).
commonErrors: leaves lines unlabeled
places the center of mass outside the gliders
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: All three lines labeled; the center of mass lies between X and Y.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Indicate whether the magnitude of the change in momentum of glider X during the collision is greater than, less than, or equal to that of glider Y. Briefly justify your answer by referencing a fundamental physics principle.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates that the magnitudes are equal.
commonErrors: indicates X’s change is greater because it is more massive

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies with Newton’s third law (equal and opposite forces for the same time, so equal and opposite impulses) or with conservation of momentum.
commonErrors: states the answer without a principle
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The gliders exert equal and opposite forces on each other for the same time, so their impulses are equal in magnitude.

sampleResponse: A X: rightward arrow 2 units; Y: rightward arrow 4 units (total 6, as before). B \(2m_0v_0 = 2m_0\left(\tfrac{1}{3}v_0\right) + m_0v_Y\), so \(v_Y = \tfrac{4}{3}v_0\) and \(K_Y = \tfrac{1}{2}m_0\left(\tfrac{4}{3}v_0\right)^2 = \tfrac{8}{9}m_0v_0^2\). C After \(t_1\): Y rises with the steepest slope \(\left(\tfrac{4}{3}v_0\right)\); X rises with slope \(\tfrac{1}{3}v_0\); the center of mass continues with the same slope \(\tfrac{2}{3}v_0\), between the two gliders. D Equal: by Newton's third law the gliders exert equal and opposite forces on each other for the same time, so their changes in momentum are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.

rubricPoints.exampleFailing: μk = F/m from the third row.

rubricPoints.criterion: Reports \(\mu_k\) between about 0.27 and 0.33.
commonErrors: forgets to divide by g, reporting about 2.9

sampleResponse: A (i) The total mass \(m\) of the block and added masses (balance) and the spring scale reading \(F\) while the block slides at constant speed. (ii) Repeat each pull three times and average, and use five different masses. B (i) \(F\) on the vertical axis, \(m\) on the horizontal axis. (ii) At constant speed \(F = \mu_k mg\), so slope \(= \mu_k g\). C Vertical axis \(F\) (N), linear scale, five plotted points, straight best-fit line. D Slope \(\approx 2.9\text{ N/kg}\), so \(\mu_k = 2.9/9.8 \approx 0.30\).

title: Pushing a Merry-Go-Round
topic: Qualitative/Quantitative Translation · Torque, rotational work, and angular speed

stimulus.content: Figure 1 (overhead view): Overhead view of a circular merry-go-round with an axle at its center. A tangential force F is applied at the outer edge, a distance R from the axle; a dashed inner circle marks the distance R/2

prompt: A playground merry-go-round has rotational inertia \(I\) about its frictionless central axle and is initially at rest. In Case 1, a student pushes on the outer edge, a distance \(R\) from the axle, with a constant force of magnitude \(F\) that is always tangent to the circular path, while the merry-go-round turns through an angle \(\theta\). In Case 2, the student pushes with the same force at a distance \(\tfrac{R}{2}\) from the axle through the same angle \(\theta\). The final angular speeds are \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\).

parts.label: A
parts.text: Indicate whether \(\omega_2\) is greater than, less than, or equal to \(\omega_1\). Justify your answer using qualitative reasoning beyond referencing equations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Indicates \(\omega_2 < \omega_1\).
commonErrors: indicates equal because the force is the same

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that pushing closer to the axle produces a smaller torque (or that the push acts over a shorter arc length, doing less work).
commonErrors: says the force is smaller closer to the center
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: At R/2 the same force has half the lever arm, so it exerts half the torque.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The force is weaker near the center.

rubricPoints.criterion: Connects the smaller torque or work over the same angle to less rotational kinetic energy (or smaller angular acceleration), and so a smaller final angular speed.
commonErrors: states the conclusion without connecting torque or work to speed
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Less work is done over the same angle, so the merry-go-round gains less rotational kinetic energy and spins more slowly.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Starting with the work-energy theorem or Newton's second law in rotational form, derive an expression for \(\omega_1\) in terms of \(I\), \(F\), \(R\), \(\theta\), and physical constants, as appropriate.

rubricPoints.criterion: Begins with the work-energy theorem \(W = \Delta K\) (or \(\tau = I\alpha\) with rotational kinematics).
commonErrors: uses linear kinetic energy ½mv²

rubricPoints.criterion: Expresses the work as \(\tau\theta = FR\theta\) (or the torque as \(FR\)) and the kinetic energy as \(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\).
commonErrors: uses Fθ without the lever arm
uses a lever arm of R/2 in Case 1

rubricPoints.criterion: Arrives at \(\omega_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2FR\theta}{I}}\).
commonErrors: drops the square root
drops the factor of 2

parts.label: C
parts.text: Indicate whether your expression from part B is or is not consistent with your reasoning in part A. Justify by referencing the expression.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses functional dependence language relating \(\omega\) to the distance from the axle (\(\omega \propto \sqrt{R}\)).
commonErrors: restates part A without referencing the expression

rubricPoints.criterion: Correctly concludes that halving the distance reduces \(\omega\) (by a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\)), consistent with part A.
commonErrors: concludes ω is halved
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Replacing \(R\) with \(R/2\) multiplies \(\omega\) by \(1/\sqrt{2}\), so \(\omega_2 < \omega_1\), consistent with part A.

sampleResponse: A \(\omega_2 < \omega_1\). Pushing at half the distance with the same force gives half the torque, and through the same angle the push acts over half the arc length, so it does half as much work. The merry-go-round gains less rotational kinetic energy, so it turns more slowly. B \(W = \Delta K\): \(FR\theta = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega_1^2\), so \(\omega_1 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2FR\theta}{I}}\). C Consistent: \(\omega \propto \sqrt{R}\), so pushing at \(R/2\) gives \(\omega_2 = \omega_1/\sqrt{2} < \omega_1\).
